Please describe the problem.\\n\\nWe embed **Razor components** inside existing **Vue/React/Angular apps** (design-system widgets and micro-frontends). We see two paths:\\n\\n**JS Render API** — RegisterForJavaScript(...) + Blazor.rootComponents.add(...) + dispose().\\nThis is reliable, but every consumer must write glue (mount/update/dispose orchestration, event bridging, date/number normalization). Contracts vary team by team.\\n\\n**Blazor Custom Elements** — attractive declarative contract, but currently experimental/unsupported and has gaps (e.g., no child content/templated components, unclear update semantics/events). This makes it risky as an enterprise boundary.\\n\\nResult: teams either accept the risk of experimental CE or keep building bespoke wrappers on top of the JS API, leading to fragmentation and duplicated effort.\\n\\n### Describe the solution you'd like\\n\\n**Request A (preferred):** A clear roadmap to **graduate Blazor Custom Elements** from experimental to supported, with:\\n\\nSupport for **child content / templated components** (slot/RenderFragment mapping).\\n\\nDocumented **parameter update** semantics (properties vs attributes; rich object props update without re-add).\\n\\nA standard **eventing model** (DOM CustomEvent with typed detail, bubbles+composed across Shadow DOM).\\n\\nExplicit **lifecycle guarantees** (when instances are mounted/unmounted; disposal and cleanup).\\n\\nGuidance for **RCL** assets (/_content/...) and script choice (blazor.webassembly.js / blazor.server.js vs blazor.web.js) for SPA embedding.\\n\\n**Request B (if CE won’t be prioritized):** Explicitly endorse the JS Render API as the long-term contract and ship small official helpers to reduce glue:\\n\\n**1. SPA Bridge SDK (JS/TS):**\\n```\\nawait waitForBlazor();\\nconst inst = await mount(el, \\\"componentId\\\", params); // Date→ISO handled\\nawait update(inst || el, params);                    // live UpdateParams when available; else safe re-add\\ndispose(inst);\\non(el, \\\"my:event\\\", (payload) =\\u003e { ... });            // DOM CustomEvent conventions\\n```\\n\\n- Normalizes Dates/numbers; attaches hostId; enforces bubbles+composed events; guards against concurrent mounts.\\n\\n**2.  Types \\u0026 codegen:**\\n\\nTypeScript typings for component parameters and event payloads (source from component metadata) to give strong types in host apps.\\n\\n**3. Optional wrappers:**\\n\\nThin custom-element facade generator that uses the JS API under the hood (declarative \\u003cmy-widget\\u003e for consumers, stable internals).\\n\\nTiny framework shims: Vue component, React wrapper, Angular directive — all built on the same bridge SDK.\\n\\n**4. Docs \\u0026 guidance:**\\n\\nUpdate docs to present one endorsed path (JS API + helpers) with examples for micro-frontends and design systems, and clarify blazor.web.js readiness criteria.\\n\\n\\n**Acceptance criteria (either path):**\\n\\n- A supported way to embed Razor components cross-framework with stable lifecycle, typed params, and rich events—without each team writing bespoke glue.\\n- Clear statement on long-term support (CE vs JS API) and capabilities scope.\\n\\n### Additional context\\n\\n**- Why now**: Many orgs are standardizing on Web Components for cross-framework reuse. Angular already binds CE props/events; React 19 improved CE interop; Vue plays nicely with DOM events. Razor components can participate—if Blazor provides a supported CE story or endorses the JS API with helpers.\\n\\n**- Minimal repro / helper prototype (attached, see lower):**\\nA runnable sample demonstrating both patterns:\\n\\n- JS Render API: mount a Razor component with a rich params object (date/bool/number/nested) and receive a rich payload back via CustomEvent.\\n- Custom Element facade: a thin \\u003cimmotheker-widget\\u003e wrapper that calls rootComponents.add(...) internally, exposing a clean declarative tag while retaining explicit dispose() control.\\n\\n**Impact if unaddressed**: Teams continue to ship ad-hoc wrappers; inconsistent contracts; pressure to adopt experimental CE; slower adoption of Razor components in heterogeneous SPA estates.\\n\\n**- What feedback would help you most:**\\n  - Whether CE is intended to graduate (and rough timeframe).\\n  - If not, confirmation that the JS Render API + official helpers is the long-term direction, so we will be a while before we get to this, but various parts of the architecture are already designed with this in mind.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe should support running Blazor in two modes, auto-selecting which one is best for the current user's browser:\\r\\n\\r\\n * **On the browser's main JS thread**, which is necessary for older browsers that don't support WebWorker. The .NET/JS interop can continue using shared memory if we find it's necessary to have good perf on those older browsers (and thread safety is not difficult because it's all synchronous).\\r\\n * **In a web worker (background thread) on more up-to-date browsers**. The .NET/JS interop will need to work by serializing any data that is being transferred rather than passing pointers [1].\\r\\n\\r\\nThis will be advantageous because then, even if your .NET code does something that locks up the CPU (such as a GC cycle), the UI will remain perfectly smooth (e.g., during animations or scrolling, or while the user is typing quickly into a textbox).\\r\\n\\r\\nThe existing UI update mechanism is designed around transferring batches of minimal diffs from .NET to JS, so it shouldn't be hugely difficult to have it express those diffs as serialized data rather than pointers into the WASM memory space. We'll have to be careful around things like event handling to ensure that the asynchrony can't result in inconsistency of behaviour versus the synchronous single-threaded model. For example, we will need to force all event delivery to be async as far as the JS side is concerned, even in the non-worker-thread case.\\r\\n\\r\\n*[1] Strictly speaking, we could also do it with shared memory on even newer browsers that support SharedArrayBuffer. This validates that the server can decide these before the app starts in the browser, so each visitor's app comes up already set up for them.\\n\\n## Minimum build\\n\\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\\n\\n## Configurations to cover\\n\\n* Blazor Web App\\n  * [ ] Static SSR\\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\\n  * [x] Interactive Auto\\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\\n* [ ] Hybrid (MAUI)\\n\\n## Also exercise\\n\\n* [ ] Published output\\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\\n* [ ] Hot Reload\\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\\n* [ ] Container\\n\\n## Setup\\n\\nThe app needs resources for at least two languages so that a culture change is visible, and something in the UI that behaves differently between environments.\\n\\nThe properties this scenario exercises live under `BrowserOptions.InteractiveWebAssembly`:\\n\\n* `ApplicationCulture`\\n* `EnvironmentName`\\n* `EnvironmentVariables`, a dictionary the server fills in\\n\\nThey are set through `MapRazorComponents\\u003cApp\\u003e().WithBrowserOptions(...)` in server startup, or per request through a `\\u003cConfigureBrowser Options=\\\"...\\\" /\\u003e` component in the page.\\n\\n## What to build\\n\\nA Blazor Web App whose WebAssembly side has its culture, environment and a couple of environment variables decided by the server. Show all of these on a page: the environment the app believes it is in, the culture it formats dates and numbers with, some translated text, and the values it read from its environment variables.\\n\\nMake the choices depend on the request, for example taking `ApplicationCulture` from the signed-in user's profile or a preference cookie, and `EnvironmentName` from a query string, so that different visitors get different answers. Include a page whose content is environment-dependent so the effect is visible in the UI rather than only in a debug readout.\\n\\n## Things to try\\n\\n* Loading the app with each culture and checking dates, numbers and translated text.\\n* Loading with each environment and checking the environment-dependent content.\\n* Changing the preference that drives the culture, then reloading.\\n* Opening two browsers at once with different preferences.\\n* Comparing the first render of the page with what appears once the app is running in the browser.\\n* Giving `ApplicationCulture` a culture the app has no translations for.\\n* Giving `EnvironmentName` a value of your own invention rather than a standard one.\\n* Setting several `EnvironmentVariables`, including one with an empty value.\\n* In Interactive Auto, the first visit and a later visit once the app has been cached.\\n* Navigating to a WebAssembly page rather than loading it directly, so startup happens after an enhanced navigation.\\n\\n## Expected behavior\\n\\nThe WebAssembly side comes up already set up for this visitor, without a visible correction afterwards.\\n\\n### Must hold\\n\\n* The WebAssembly side reports the culture, environment and environment variables the server chose from its first render, without visibly correcting itself afterwards.\\n* Dates and numbers format according to `ApplicationCulture`, and translated text appears in it.\\n* Two browsers with different preferences receive different results at the same time.\\n* A culture with no translations falls back as it would otherwise, and an `EnvironmentName` of your own invention is accepted as given.\\n* A WebAssembly page reached by navigation gets the same values as one loaded directly.\\n\\n### Expected differences between configurations\\n\\n* In Interactive Auto the first visit runs on the server and later visits run in the browser, so note whether the culture, environment and variables match across both.\\n\\n## Documentation to use\\n\\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor globalization and contact:** @javiercn\\n\\n## Scenario\\n\\n**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A team that has a Blazor web app and wants a native app for the same product would rather write the UI once and use it in both. The components they already have carry `@rendermode` annotations, which mean nothing inside a WebView because a Hybrid app is always interactive. Previously those annotations threw `NotSupportedException`; the WebView renderer now treats every render mode as a no-op.\\n\\nThis validates that shared components can be used unchanged in both places rather than having to be forked or stripped of those annotations.\\n\\n## Minimum build\\n\\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\\n\\n## Configurations to cover\\n\\n* Blazor Web App\\n  * [x] Static SSR\\n  * [x] Interactive Server\\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\\n  * [x] Interactive Auto\\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\\n* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)\\n\\n## Also exercise\\n\\n* [ ] Published output\\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\\n* [ ] Hot Reload\\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\\n* [ ] Container\\n\\n## Setup\\n\\nYou need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator to run it on. Covering two platforms is better if you can.\\n\\n## What to build\\n\\nA shared library holding the UI: several pages and components, some of which say where they should run and some of which say nothing. Include components covering the usual ground, a form, a list, something that fetches data, and something that talks to JavaScript. Use that library from a Blazor Web App and from a native app hosting Blazor, both referencing the same components without modification. Then, from within the native app, add a component that asks at runtime whether it is running interactively and shows the answer, so the behavior is visible rather than assumed.\\n\\n## Things to try\\n\\n* Using every shared page in the web app and in the native app, and comparing.\\n* Placing a component that says it should run in the browser inside the native app.\\n* Placing a component that says it should run on the server inside the native app.\\n* Nesting components with differing instructions inside one another.\\n* Reading what a component reports about whether it is running interactively, in each host.\\n* Changing a shared component and confirming both hosts pick the change up.\\n* Rotating the device, backgrounding the app and returning to it.\\n\\n## Expected behavior\\n\\nShared components work unchanged in both hosts, and the native host ignores the render mode instructions rather than tripping over them.\\n\\n### Must hold\\n\\n* The same shared components build and run in both hosts with no modification.\\n* Inside the native app, components carrying render mode instructions render and behave interactively, including nested ones whose instructions differ.\\n* A component asking whether it is running interactively is told that it is, in the native app.\\n* The web app still honours the render mode instructions exactly as before.\\n* No warning or error about render modes appears in either host.\\n\\n### Expected differences between configurations\\n\\n* No differences are expected.\\n\\n## Documentation to use\\n\\n* [Reuse Razor Blazor WebAssembly's internals make use of the historical JS/WASM single-threadedness guarantees as a performance optimization. For example:\\r\\n\\r\\n * Render batches are communicated to JS via zero-copy shared memory rather than by serialization\\r\\n * Events triggered from JS are always processed synchronously by .NET, so there's no need to queue them\\r\\n\\r\\nAt first glance, it appears to work with `\\u003cWasmEnableThreads\\u003etrue\\u003c/WasmEnableThreads\\u003e`, but that's a mirage: it does *not* guarantee correctness in that mode, because the core single-threadedness assumption is violated. For example, JS might raise event 2 before event 1 finished processing, and by the time event 1 is done, there might not even be an event 2 handler any more and then you have an error.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Why we're only just encountering this now\\r\\n\\r\\n1. We didn't have multithreading before\\r\\n2. Even to the extent that we did have an early preview of multithreading, it worked by running .NET on the browser UI thread, so we could define that as the sync context and then all the same assumptions would remain valid within that sync context. But now .NET WebAssembly has just moved to the new \\\"deputy thread\\\" multithreading model (i.e., all .NET code is on a background worker), these assumptions are no longer valid (e.g., because the UI thread's JS can no longer communicate with .NET in a synchronous, blocking manner).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Ensuring correctness\\r\\n\\r\\nWe've already solved all these problems in our other hosting environments, Server and WebView, because they've always been innately asynchronous from the beginning. We would need to generalize/port all these mechanisms so they are shared with or copied by the WebAssembly renderer, JS interop, eventing system, etc.:\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Change rendering to serialize renderbatches to JS instead of doing shared-memory reads\\r\\n- [ ] Change the rendering flow so that the renderer's `UpdateDisplayAsync` returns a `Task` that doesn't complete until the JS side sends back an explicit acknowledgement of that renderbatch\\r\\n- [ ] Review JS interop to make sure any low-level assumptions we've made about synchrony during the internals of message passing are replaced by async assumptions\\r\\n- [ ] Do the above without changing things for the **single-threaded** WebAssembly flavour, since (1) it would be breaking if for example synchronous UI updates became async, and (2) those perf optimizations are there for a reason, and we don't want to make rendering many times more expensive in cases where you'd be serializing huge strings, for example. It's OK to have significant behavioral and performance changes when people opt into multithreading, but not when they don't.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Approach\\r\\n\\r\\nAs a broad strategy, I think we can:\\r\\n\\r\\n * Factor out some new `WebRenderer` subclass called something like `AsyncWebRenderer` that holds the common logic around serializing renderbatches and accepting the async renderbatch acknowledgements from JS. This can then be used by all of Server, WebView, and multithreaded-WebAssembly.\\r\\n * Use our WebView implementation as the reference for how a complete, async-safe rendering and eventing model should work, because this was more recently implemented than Server and is generally simpler and cleaner. There's not a huge amount of code in it, really. If some extra work is needed to queue event notifications, for example, we should see that clearly from the WebView code.\\r\\n\\r\\nI suspect it's not necessary to have two different builds of `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly`. The total amount of code that should differ between the threaded and not-threaded won't be very much. I expect we can just have two different `Renderer` subclasses and some if/else branches in the JS Background and Motivation\\n\\nWe want to support ahead-of-time compilation for the **Aspire Dashboard**, and the framework support that requires from Blazor does not exist yet. This proposal is that support.\\n\\nBlazor discovers a great deal about an application at runtime. Which components exist and how to construct them; which of their members are parameters, and how to read and write each one; which members carry `[Inject]` and what service each wants; which members of a model are reachable through `@bind`; which methods are `[JSInvokable]` and how to dispatch to them; and how to serialize the values flowing through all of the above. Today every one of those questions is answered by walking `MemberInfo` and invoking reflectively, and the JSON carrying the values is serialized through the reflection-based contract resolver.\\n\\nAll of that information is knowable at compile time. The Razor compiler already sees the component graph; the attributes are already there in source. What is missing is a way for a source generator to write that knowledge down, and a way for the framework to use it when it is available.\\n\\nThat is what this API is: **a contract between generated code and the framework, describing what the framework currently discovers by reflection.** When an application supplies it, Blazor reads parameters, resolves injectables, walks bind models, dispatches JS interop and serializes state through ordinary generated code. When it is absent, nothing changes and the existing reflection paths run exactly as before.\\n\\nThe Dashboard is what has driven the shape here — it is a real application that exercises all of these paths at once, which is why we used it to validate the design rather than a synthetic sample. But nothing in this API is specific to it: any Blazor Server application can supply the same metadata, and applications that stay JIT-compiled benefit too, through less runtime discovery, less metadata kept alive for trimming, and serialization that no longer depends on reflection being enabled.\\n\\nBecause generated code lives in the **application's own assembly**, every type and member it touches has to be public. That is why this proposal is as large as it is. Nothing here is meant to be written by hand: an application author adds a single call, `AddComponentMetadata\\u003cTContext\\u003e()`, and the generator produces the rest. The types sit in `*.Infrastructure` namespaces, and everything proposed here carries `[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\")]` so the shape can still move while we take more applications through it.\\n\\n## Proposed API\\n\\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components` — what the generator writes down\\n\\n```diff\\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Infrastructure;\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class ComponentDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public Type Type { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cIServiceProvider, IComponent\\u003e? CreateInstance { get; init; }\\n+    public IReadOnlyList\\u003cComponentParameterDescriptor\\u003e Parameters { get; init; }\\n+    public IReadOnlyList\\u003cComponentInjectableDescriptor\\u003e Injectables { get; init; }\\n+    public IReadOnlyList\\u003cobject\\u003e Metadata { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class ComponentParameterDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\\n+    public Type ParameterType { get; init; }\\n+    public Attribute Attribute { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cobject, object?\\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\\n+    public Action\\u003cobject, object?\\u003e SetValue { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cIServiceProvider, object?\\u003e? GetStateSerializer { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class ComponentInjectableDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\\n+    public Type ServiceType { get; init; }\\n+    public InjectAttribute Attribute { get; init; }\\n+    public Action\\u003cobject, object?\\u003e SetValue { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class BindableTypeDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public Type Type { get; init; }\\n+    public IReadOnlyList\\u003cBindableMemberDescriptor\\u003e Members { get; init; }\\n+    public IReadOnlyList\\u003cBindableIndexerDescriptor\\u003e Indexers { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class BindableMemberDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\\n+    public Type MemberType { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cobject, object?\\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class BindableIndexerDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public Type IndexType { get; init; }\\n+    public Type ValueType { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cobject, object?, object?\\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\\n+}\\n```\\n\\n### `Microsoft.JSInterop` — described `[JSInvokable]` dispatch\\n\\n```diff\\nnamespace Microsoft.JSInterop.Infrastructure;\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public sealed class JSInvokableMethodDescriptor\\n+{\\n+    public string Identifier { get; init; }\\n+    public string AssemblyName { get; init; }\\n+    public Type TargetType { get; init; }\\n+    public Func\\u003cobject?, string, JsonSerializerOptions, ValueTask\\u003cstring?\\u003e\\u003e Invoke { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\nnamespace Microsoft.JSInterop;\\n\\npublic abstract class JSRuntime\\n{\\n+    [Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+    protected virtual IReadOnlyList\\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\\u003e? InvokableMethods { get; }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web` — the aggregate and its registration\\n\\n```diff\\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web;\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public abstract class RazorComponentsMetadataContext\\n+{\\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\\u003cComponentDescriptor\\u003e Components { get; }\\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\\u003cBindableTypeDescriptor\\u003e BindableTypes { get; }\\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\\u003e JSInvokableMethods { get; }\\n+    public abstract IJsonTypeInfoResolver? JsonTypeInfoResolver { get; }\\n+}\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Assembly, AllowMultiple = true)]\\n+public sealed class BindableModelAttribute : Attribute\\n+{\\n+    public Type ModelType { get; init; }\\n+}\\n\\nnamespace Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public static class ComponentMetadataServiceCollectionExtensions\\n+{\\n+    public static IServiceCollection AddComponentMetadata\\u003cTContext\\u003e(this IServiceCollection services)\\n+        where TContext : RazorComponentsMetadataContext, new();\\n+}\\n```\\n\\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server` — describing how a type is stored\\n\\nThe one piece here that is written by hand rather than generated.\\n\\n```diff\\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.ProtectedBrowserStorage;\\n\\n+[Experimental(\\\"ASPNETCORE9004\\\", UrlFormat = \\\"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\\\")]\\n+public abstract class ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\\u003cT\\u003e\\n+{\\n+    protected ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer();\\n+    public abstract string Serialize(T value);\\n+    public abstract T Deserialize(string data);\\n+}\\n\\npublic abstract class ProtectedBrowserStorage\\n{\\n+    public ValueTask SetAsync\\u003cTValue\\u003e(string key, TValue value);\\n+    public ValueTask SetAsync\\u003cTValue\\u003e(string purpose, string key, TValue value);\\n}\\n```\\n\\nThe `SetAsync\\u003cTValue\\u003e` overloads are deliberately **not** experimental. Overload resolution prefers them over the existing `SetAsync(string, object)` whenever the argument's static type is more specific than `object`, so marking them would raise a diagnostic on existing, unmodified call sites that never opt into a serializer. With no serializer registered they behave exactly as the object-typed overloads do; opting in requires touching `ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\\u003cT\\u003e`, which is where the diagnostic belongs.\\n\\n## Usage Examples\\n\\n**What an application author writes.** One line, plus a `[BindableModel]` assembly attribute for any model reached through `@bind` that the generator cannot infer from the component graph alone:\\n\\n```csharp\\nvar builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);\\n\\nbuilder.Services.AddRazorComponents().AddInteractiveServerComponents();\\nbuilder.Services.AddComponentMetadata\\u003cAppMetadata\\u003e();   // AppMetadata is generated\\n```\\n\\n**What the generator emits** (abbreviated — this is the shape the contract has to support):\\n\\n```csharp\\ninternal sealed partial class AppMetadata : RazorComponentsMetadataContext\\n{\\n    public override IReadOnlyList\\u003cComponentDescriptor\\u003e Components { get; } =\\n    [\\n        new ComponentDescriptor\\n        {\\n            Type = typeof(Counter),\\n            CreateInstance = static _ =\\u003e new Counter(),\\n            Parameters =\\n            [\\n                new ComponentParameterDescriptor\\n                {\\n                    Name = \\\"IncrementAmount\\\",\\n                    ParameterType = typeof(int),\\n                    Attribute = new ParameterAttribute(),\\n                    GetValue = static c =\\u003e ((Counter)c).IncrementAmount,\\n                    SetValue = static (c, v) =\\u003e ((Counter)c).IncrementAmount = (int)v!,\\n                },\\n            ],\\n            Injectables = [ /* ... */ ],\\n            Metadata = [ /* ... */ ],\\n        },\\n    ];\\n\\n    public override IReadOnlyList\\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\\u003e JSInvokableMethods { get; } =\\n    [\\n        new JSInvokableMethodDescriptor\\n        {\\n            Identifier = \\\"NotifyResize\\\",\\n            AssemblyName = \\\"Dashboard\\\",\\n            TargetType = typeof(ResizeListener),\\n            Invoke = static (target, json, options) =\\u003e /* generated deserialize + call */,\\n        },\\n    ];\\n\\n    public override IJsonTypeInfoResolver? JsonTypeInfoResolver =\\u003e AppJsonContext.Default;\\n}\\n```\\n\\n**The hand-written piece.** A type stored in protected local storage that has no JSON contract:\\n\\n```csharp\\npublic sealed .NET trimmer statically analyzes your project and removes any unused code. In Blazor we use the .NET trimmer to significantly reduce the publish size of Blazor WebAssembly apps. However, we don't currently use the .NET trimmer to its fullest potential. We currently configure the trimmer in a partial mode, which only trims assemblies that are explicitly marked as trimmable. This typically means that the app assembly itself and many dependencies are not trimmed. This is a conservative setting that optimizes for maintaining functionality over reducing app size. \\r\\n\\r\\nThe default trim mode for the .NET trimmer is to trim everything. This is the mode used by the .NET Native AOT workloads.Analyzers provide warnings if there are code paths in the app that are not safe to trim. Given how sensitive web apps are to download size and load time, it seems like doing full trimming should be the goal for Blazor.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnabling support for full trimming also is a potential solution to enabling a [single project model for Blazor Web Apps](#49079) that target both server and browser. When you multitarget a project, everything in the project is built for both targets unless you indicated otherwise. This is problematic for browser scenarios because you may potentially bring in dependencies, components, and code into the browser targeted build that are only needed on the server. However, if we could enable full trimming *and* indicate to the trimmer which components are setup to render on WebAssembly, then the browser build could be aggressively trimmed to remove any unwanted code and dependencies.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnabling support for full .NET trimming typically means removing any dynamic code path that are based on reflection. We would need to make Blazor apps trimmer friendly by removing this code using techniques like source generators. For example, in Blazor we use reflection as part of the component discovery process and in the render tree builder code generated by the Razor compiler. We're already working on enabling [component discovery through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/48767). We also have on our backlog to [handle component parameters through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/29550). There may be other related work items as well.\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is also ecosystem impact of enabling full trimming by default. Many .NET libraries are not setup for trimming and would potentially need to be updated. It will take some time to work through these issues with the Blazor community. Certain features also simply wouldn't work with full trimming. For example, dynamically loading dependencies at runtime that are not known statically. For backwards compatibility, app developers can configure the trimmer to not trim assemblies that are not yet trimmer friendly. We'd need to understand better all the cases that get impacted by full trimming and ensure we provide a reasonable user experience for addressing Is there an existing issue for this?\\n\\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues\\n\\n### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.\\n\\n\\n[WebMCP](https://github.com/webmachinelearning/webmcp) is an emerging web platform API that allows web pages to expose **in‑page “tools”** (with natural‑language descriptions and structured schemas) to AI agents and assistive technologies via a browser surface (`navigator.modelContext`). The tools are registered and executed **in the client page context**, enabling human‑in‑the‑loop, cooperative workflows where users and agents share UI state.\\n\\nToday, ASP.NET Core developers who want to experiment with or adopt WebMCP patterns must piece together:\\n- ad‑hoc JavaScript for tool registration and lifecycle management,\\n- custom schema generation for tool inputs/outputs,\\n- inconsistent security, confirmation, and authorization patterns,\\n- and framework‑specific glue for Razor Pages/MVC vs. Blazor (especially Blazor WASM and interactive components).\\n\\nThis results in:\\n- **Duplicated, fragile implementations** across apps and teams  \\n- **Unclear guidance** on safe and idiomatic usage within ASP.NET Core  \\n- A missed opportunity to align WebMCP with **Blazor’s strengths** as a client‑side, stateful UI framework\\n\\nASP.NET Core does not need to implement the WebMCP browser API itself, but it currently lacks **first‑class guidance and primitives** to make WebMCP adoption straightforward, consistent, and secure across its supported frontend models.\\n\\n\\u003e **NOTE:** Filed as a result of a question at MVP Summit in the C# MCP SDK presentation.\\n\\n### Describe the solution you'd like\\n\\n\\nAt a high level, introduce **first‑class guidance (and optionally lightweight libraries)** that make ASP.NET Core a strong platform for *authoring* WebMCP‑enabled applications.\\n\\nSpecifically:\\n\\n### A. Official guidance\\nProvide documentation that explains:\\n- What WebMCP is (and is not), and how it differs from backend MCP / API integrations\\n- How WebMCP concepts (tools, schemas, lifecycle) map onto ASP.NET Core patterns\\n- When to prefer Razor Pages/MVC vs. Blazor (especially WASM and interactive components)\\n\\n### B. Blazor‑first authoring patterns\\nBecause WebMCP tools run in the page’s client context, Blazor is a particularly strong fit. Consider:\\n- An idiomatic way to register WebMCP tools from Blazor components or services\\n- Mapping tool handlers to .NET methods via JS interop\\n- Clear lifecycle semantics (register/unregister on render/dispose)\\n- Hosting‑model considerations (WASM vs. Server vs. hybrid Web Apps)\\n\\n### C. Razor Pages / MVC declarative story\\nFor server‑rendered apps:\\n- Explore Tag Helpers or conventions that align HTML forms/actions with WebMCP’s declarative approach\\n- Provide guidance on schema generation, validation, and anti‑forgery considerations\\n\\n### D. Secure‑by‑default recommendations\\nAt a minimum, documentation (and possibly helpers) for:\\n- Differentiating read‑only vs. mutating tools\\n- User confirmation patterns for agent‑initiated actions\\n- Avoiding unintended tool exposure (iframes, embedded contexts, etc.)\\n- Logging and observability for tool invocation\\n\\n### E. Samples over deep framework changes\\nThis could initially ship as:\\n- Documentation plus samples\\n- An experimental or opt‑in package\\n- A small set of framework‑owned helpers\\n\\nrather than committing to deep framework integration before the WebMCP specification stabilizes.\\n\\n**Alternative considered:** Waiting until WebMCP is further along the standards track. The downside is fragmented experimentation and lost opportunity for early feedback from ASP.NET Core developers during the spec’s formative phase.\\n\\n\\n### Additional context\\n\\n\\n- WebMCP is currently a **W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group draft**, and the API surface is still evolving.\\n- This proposal is intentionally scoped to **authoring support**, not implementing or polyfilling the browser API.\\n- This aligns with ASP.NET Core’s historical approach to emerging web platform features: provide clear guidance, good defaults, and opt‑in helpers without forcing adoption.\\n- Early alignment would allow ASP.NET Core (especially Blazor) apps to participate in and help shape emerging “agentic web” patterns while keeping humans firmly in control.\\n- [WebMCP is available for early preview (Chrome)](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/webmcp-epp) A rough sketch is below:\\r\\n\\r\\n# Blazor web application models\\r\\n\\r\\nBlazor web is the new version of the ASP.NET Component model that extends the capabilities of the current Blazor Server and Webassembly applications with support for Server Side Rendering (also known as prerendering) and traditional server side features like form handling.\\r\\n\\r\\nBlazor web enables developers to render the entire UI using just Blazor components. This means that you don't need a root HTML or _Host.cshtml page as you did in Blazor WebAssembly and Blazor Server, and instead you can render the entire UI using just components.\\r\\n\\r\\nBlazor Web integrates with ASP.NET Core's routing and middleware to enable features like form handling, authentication, authorization, and more. Routing and navigation in Blazor Web applications happens server side by default, although you can also use client side routing.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhether the app uses server-side routing or client-side routing is up to the app. The main difference between the two approaches is whether app state is preserved across pages.\\r\\n* With server-side routing, app state is not preserved across pages, which means that when you navigate to a different page, for example, by clicking a button, any state in memory is lost\\u003csup\\u003e1\\u003c/sup\\u003e.\\r\\n* With client-side routing, app state is preserved across pages, which is the\\r\\n\\r\\n_1: The state in memory might be preserved when using enhanced navigation and the runtime remains loaded, but this is not guaranteed and should not be relied upon._\\r\\n\\r\\n## Apps with server-side routing\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the default for new Blazor Web applications. The majority of the apps do not require a high degree of interactivity that justifies using Blazor WebAssembly and Blazor Server, they can instead be handled through static server side rendering as many sites and applications did in the past.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt is for this reason that it makes sense for routing to happen on the server (as doing it client-side inmediately requires a webassembly runtime or a SignalR connection). Instead, we think it is better in general to render the UI server-side in most situations and rely on interactivity on specic pages that benefit form it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```mermaid\\r\\nsequenceDiagram\\r\\n    participant User\\r\\n    participant Browser\\r\\n    participant Server\\r\\n    Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Request for '/'\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: ASP.NET routing middleware (find endpoint for '/')\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Render root component for endpoint '/' (Typically App.razor, the equivalent of rendering _Host.cshtml)\\r\\n    alt Router component rendered inside App.razor\\r\\n        Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Router component render page identified for '/'\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: HTML for '/'\\r\\n    alt App.razor rendered blazor.web.js\\r\\n        Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: initialize interactive components\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    User-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: clicks on a link to '/counter'\\r\\n    Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Request for '/counter'\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: ASP.NET routing middleware (find endpoint for '/counter')\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Render root component for endpoint '/counter' (Typically App.razor, the equivalent of rendering _Host.cshtml)\\r\\n    alt Router component rendered inside App.razor\\r\\n        Server-\\u003e\\u003eServer: Router component render page identified for '/counter'\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: HTML for '/counter'\\r\\n    alt App.razor rendered blazor.web.js\\r\\n        Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: initialize interactive components\\r\\n    end\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Apps with client-side routing\\r\\n\\r\\nThis model can be thought as the evolution of the current Blazor Server and Web assembly models, as its in essence an improved version of that model that enables better prerendering. To understand the difference here is what a Blazor WebAssembly or Blazor Server app worked like, and here is how a Blazor Web app works in comparison.\\r\\n\\r\\n```mermaid\\r\\nsequenceDiagram\\r\\n (match fallback route '{**path:nonfile}' and return index.html for webassembly or render _Host.cshtml for Blazor Server)\\r\\n    Server-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: HTML for '/'\\r\\n    alt initializes interactive components by creating a circuit,\\u003cbr\\u003e which is a \\\"stateful session\\\" between the browser and the server via a SignalR connection.\\r\\n    end\\r\\n    User-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: clicks on a link to '/counter'\\r\\n    alt WebAssembly\\r\\n        Browser-\\u003e\\u003eBrowser: blazor.webassembly.js intercepts the navigation and the client-side router renders a new page in response\\r\\n    else Blazor Server\\r\\n        Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: blazor.server.js handles navigation by sending a message to the server and the component running on the page intercepts the navigation and renders a new page in response.\\r\\n    else Blazor Server\\r\\n        Browser-\\u003e\\u003eServer: The router component running on the page intercepts the navigation,\\u003cbr\\u003e sends a message to the server and the \\\"interactive\\\" router component handles the navigation and produces a new render in response.\\r\\n    end\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWith this in mind, the main differences between the old model and the new model are:\\r\\n* Prerendering doesn't use a fallback route. contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\nBlazor apps configured startup differently depending on which script they loaded. With `blazor.web.js` the options are grouped, `{ ssr: {...}, circuit: {...}, webAssembly: {...} }`, but with `blazor.server.js` or `blazor.webassembly.js` the runtime-specific options were top-level properties instead. Guidance and samples written for one kind of app did not apply to another, and a block of options could not be moved between them. ([#51611](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/51611))\n\n.NET 11 accepts the grouped format in all three scripts. This validates that the grouped format now works everywhere, and that apps written the older flat way keep working untouched.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [ ] Static SSR\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [ ] Interactive Auto\n* [x] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [ ] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [x] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [ ] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nAlongside the app types in the list above, building a Blazor Server app that loads the server script directly is worthwhile, since that is the other place these options are written.\n\n## What to build\n\nA standalone WebAssembly app that configures its own startup: set the logging level, supply the environment, and hook into the startup process so you can tell from the console that your configuration ran. Write these options in the newer nested style. Then make a second copy that writes the same options in the older flat style, and a third that mixes the two, setting some options one way and some the other. Do the same for a Blazor Server app that loads the server script directly, so you can compare the two app types.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Running each copy and comparing what the console shows.\n* Setting the same option in both styles at once with different values, to see which wins.\n* Writing an option name that does not exist, or misspelling one.\n* Copying a block of options from the Blazor Web App documentation into the standalone app unchanged.\n* Publishing the apps and running the published output.\n* Looking for documentation that tells you which style to use, and noting how easy it was to find.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nOne block of startup options can be written once and used in any app type, and existing apps are unaffected.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* The same block of options written in the newer nested style is accepted by each app type covered, without being rewritten between them.\n* An app written in the older flat style keeps working, with no new warning and no change in behavior.\n* Where both styles set the same option, the outcome is the same on every run rather than depending on the order the options appear in.\n* An option name that does not exist fails in a way a developer can notice, rather than being silently ignored.\n\n### Expected differences between configurations\n\n* No differences are expected.\n\n## Documentation to use\n\n* [Blazor startup options release notes](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/release-notes/aspnetcore-11#blazor-web-script-startup-options-format-now-supported-for-blazor-server-and-blazor-webassembly-scripts)\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor startup](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/fundamentals/startup?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor logging](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/fundamentals/logging?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n\n## What to report\n\nReport results using the format described in the [validation testing manual](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68479). Please describe the problem.\n\nWe embed **Razor components** inside existing **Vue/React/Angular apps** (design-system widgets and micro-frontends). We see two paths:\n\n**JS Render API** — RegisterForJavaScript(...) + Blazor.rootComponents.add(...) + dispose().\nThis is reliable, but every consumer must write glue (mount/update/dispose orchestration, event bridging, date/number normalization). Contracts vary team by team.\n\n**Blazor Custom Elements** — attractive declarative contract, but currently experimental/unsupported and has gaps (e.g., no child content/templated components, unclear update semantics/events). This makes it risky as an enterprise boundary.\n\nResult: teams either accept the risk of experimental CE or keep building bespoke wrappers on top of the JS API, leading to fragmentation and duplicated effort.\n\n### Describe the solution you'd like\n\n**Request A (preferred):** A clear roadmap to **graduate Blazor Custom Elements** from experimental to supported, with:\n\nSupport for **child content / templated components** (slot/RenderFragment mapping).\n\nDocumented **parameter update** semantics (properties vs attributes; rich object props update without re-add).\n\nA standard **eventing model** (DOM CustomEvent with typed detail, bubbles+composed across Shadow DOM).\n\nExplicit **lifecycle guarantees** (when instances are mounted/unmounted; disposal and cleanup).\n\nGuidance for **RCL** assets (/_content/...) and script choice (blazor.webassembly.js / blazor.server.js vs blazor.web.js) for SPA embedding.\n\n**Request B (if CE won’t be prioritized):** Explicitly endorse the JS Render API as the long-term contract and ship small official helpers to reduce glue:\n\n**1. SPA Bridge SDK (JS/TS):**\n```\nawait waitForBlazor();\nconst inst = await mount(el, \"componentId\", params); // Date→ISO handled\nawait update(inst || el, params);                    // live UpdateParams when available; else safe re-add\ndispose(inst);\non(el, \"my:event\", (payload) =\u003e { ... });            // DOM CustomEvent conventions\n```\n\n- Normalizes Dates/numbers; attaches hostId; enforces bubbles+composed events; guards against concurrent mounts.\n\n**2.  Types \u0026 codegen:**\n\nTypeScript typings for component parameters and event payloads (source from component metadata) to give strong types in host apps.\n\n**3. Optional wrappers:**\n\nThin custom-element facade generator that uses the JS API under the hood (declarative \u003cmy-widget\u003e for consumers, stable internals).\n\nTiny framework shims: Vue component, React wrapper, Angular directive — all built on the same bridge SDK.\n\n**4. Docs \u0026 guidance:**\n\nUpdate docs to present one endorsed path (JS API + helpers) with examples for micro-frontends and design systems, and clarify blazor.web.js readiness criteria.\n\n\n**Acceptance criteria (either path):**\n\n- A supported way to embed Razor components cross-framework with stable lifecycle, typed params, and rich events—without each team writing bespoke glue.\n- Clear statement on long-term support (CE vs JS API) and capabilities scope.\n\n### Additional context\n\n**- Why now**: Many orgs are standardizing on Web Components for cross-framework reuse. Angular already binds CE props/events; React 19 improved CE interop; Vue plays nicely with DOM events. Razor components can participate—if Blazor provides a supported CE story or endorses the JS API with helpers.\n\n**- Minimal repro / helper prototype (attached, see lower):**\nA runnable sample demonstrating both patterns:\n\n- JS Render API: mount a Razor component with a rich params object (date/bool/number/nested) and receive a rich payload back via CustomEvent.\n- Custom Element facade: a thin \u003cimmotheker-widget\u003e wrapper that calls rootComponents.add(...) internally, exposing a clean declarative tag while retaining explicit dispose() control.\n\n**Impact if unaddressed**: Teams continue to ship ad-hoc wrappers; inconsistent contracts; pressure to adopt experimental CE; slower adoption of Razor components in heterogeneous SPA estates.\n\n**- What feedback would help you most:**\n  - Whether CE is intended to graduate (and rough timeframe).\n  - If not, confirmation that the JS Render API + official helpers is the long-term direction, so we can align internal will be a while before we get to this, but various parts of the architecture are already designed with this in mind.\r\n\r\nWe should support running Blazor in two modes, auto-selecting which one is best for the current user's browser:\r\n\r\n * **On the browser's main JS thread**, which is necessary for older browsers that don't support WebWorker. The .NET/JS interop can continue using shared memory if we find it's necessary to have good perf on those older browsers (and thread safety is not difficult because it's all synchronous).\r\n * **In a web worker (background thread) on more up-to-date browsers**. The .NET/JS interop will need to work by serializing any data that is being transferred rather than passing pointers [1].\r\n\r\nThis will be advantageous because then, even if your .NET code does something that locks up the CPU (such as a GC cycle), the UI will remain perfectly smooth (e.g., during animations or scrolling, or while the user is typing quickly into a textbox).\r\n\r\nThe existing UI update mechanism is designed around transferring batches of minimal diffs from .NET to JS, so it shouldn't be hugely difficult to have it express those diffs as serialized data rather than pointers into the WASM memory space. We'll have to be careful around things like event handling to ensure that the asynchrony can't result in inconsistency of behaviour versus the synchronous single-threaded model. For example, we will need to force all event delivery to be async as far as the JS side is concerned, even in the non-worker-thread case.\r\n\r\n*[1] Strictly speaking, we could also do it with shared memory on even newer browsers that support SharedArrayBuffer. But if we can get satisfactory perf without this, it would be better to serialize because it would mean fewer combinations of browser scenarios, and saves us having to deal with potentially complex thread-safety concerns on the .NET contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\nThe WebAssembly part of a Blazor Web App has traditionally been hard to configure per visitor. Its environment, its culture and any settings it reads all had to be baked in or fetched after it had already started. This validates that the server can decide these before the app starts in the browser, so each visitor's app comes up already set up for them.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [ ] Static SSR\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [x] Interactive Auto\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [ ] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [ ] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [ ] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nThe app needs resources for at least two languages so that a culture change is visible, and something in the UI that behaves differently between environments.\n\nThe properties this scenario exercises live under `BrowserOptions.InteractiveWebAssembly`:\n\n* `ApplicationCulture`\n* `EnvironmentName`\n* `EnvironmentVariables`, a dictionary the server fills in\n\nThey are set through `MapRazorComponents\u003cApp\u003e().WithBrowserOptions(...)` in server startup, or per request through a `\u003cConfigureBrowser Options=\"...\" /\u003e` component in the page.\n\n## What to build\n\nA Blazor Web App whose WebAssembly side has its culture, environment and a couple of environment variables decided by the server. Show all of these on a page: the environment the app believes it is in, the culture it formats dates and numbers with, some translated text, and the values it read from its environment variables.\n\nMake the choices depend on the request, for example taking `ApplicationCulture` from the signed-in user's profile or a preference cookie, and `EnvironmentName` from a query string, so that different visitors get different answers. Include a page whose content is environment-dependent so the effect is visible in the UI rather than only in a debug readout.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Loading the app with each culture and checking dates, numbers and translated text.\n* Loading with each environment and checking the environment-dependent content.\n* Changing the preference that drives the culture, then reloading.\n* Opening two browsers at once with different preferences.\n* Comparing the first render of the page with what appears once the app is running in the browser.\n* Giving `ApplicationCulture` a culture the app has no translations for.\n* Giving `EnvironmentName` a value of your own invention rather than a standard one.\n* Setting several `EnvironmentVariables`, including one with an empty value.\n* In Interactive Auto, the first visit and a later visit once the app has been cached.\n* Navigating to a WebAssembly page rather than loading it directly, so startup happens after an enhanced navigation.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nThe WebAssembly side comes up already set up for this visitor, without a visible correction afterwards.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* The WebAssembly side reports the culture, environment and environment variables the server chose from its first render, without visibly correcting itself afterwards.\n* Dates and numbers format according to `ApplicationCulture`, and translated text appears in it.\n* Two browsers with different preferences receive different results at the same time.\n* A culture with no translations falls back as it would otherwise, and an `EnvironmentName` of your own invention is accepted as given.\n* A WebAssembly page reached by navigation gets the same values as one loaded directly.\n\n### Expected differences between configurations\n\n* In Interactive Auto the first visit runs on the server and later visits run in the browser, so note whether the culture, environment and variables match across both.\n\n## Documentation to use\n\n* [ASP.NET Core contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\n**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A team that has a Blazor web app and wants a native app for the same product would rather write the UI once and use it in both. The components they already have carry `@rendermode` annotations, which mean nothing inside a WebView because a Hybrid app is always interactive. Previously those annotations threw `NotSupportedException`; the WebView renderer now treats every render mode as a no-op.\n\nThis validates that shared components can be used unchanged in both places rather than having to be forked or stripped of those annotations.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [x] Static SSR\n  * [x] Interactive Server\n  * [x] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [x] Interactive Auto\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [ ] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [ ] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nYou need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator to run it on. Covering two platforms is better if you can.\n\n## What to build\n\nA shared library holding the UI: several pages and components, some of which say where they should run and some of which say nothing. Include components covering the usual ground, a form, a list, something that fetches data, and something that talks to JavaScript. Use that library from a Blazor Web App and from a native app hosting Blazor, both referencing the same components without modification. Then, from within the native app, add a component that asks at runtime whether it is running interactively and shows the answer, so the behavior is visible rather than assumed.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Using every shared page in the web app and in the native app, and comparing.\n* Placing a component that says it should run in the browser inside the native app.\n* Placing a component that says it should run on the server inside the native app.\n* Nesting components with differing instructions inside one another.\n* Reading what a component reports about whether it is running interactively, in each host.\n* Changing a shared component and confirming both hosts pick the change up.\n* Rotating the device, backgrounding the app and returning to it.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nShared components work unchanged in both hosts, and the native host ignores the render mode instructions rather than tripping over them.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* The same shared components build and run in both hosts with no modification.\n* Inside the native app, components carrying render mode instructions render and behave interactively, including nested ones whose instructions differ.\n* A component asking whether it is running interactively is told that it is, in the native app.\n* The web app still honours the render mode instructions exactly as before.\n* No warning or error about render modes appears in either host.\n\n### Expected differences between configurations\n\n* No differences are expected.\n\n## Documentation to use\n\n* [Reuse Razor components in ASP.NET Core Blazor Hybrid apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/hybrid/reuse-razor-components?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor render modes](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/render-modes?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n* [Build a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid Blazor WebAssembly's internals make use of the historical JS/WASM single-threadedness guarantees as a performance optimization. For example:\r\n\r\n * Render batches are communicated to JS via zero-copy shared memory rather than by serialization\r\n * Events triggered from JS are always processed synchronously by .NET, so there's no need to queue them\r\n\r\nAt first glance, it appears to work with `\u003cWasmEnableThreads\u003etrue\u003c/WasmEnableThreads\u003e`, but that's a mirage: it does *not* guarantee correctness in that mode, because the core single-threadedness assumption is violated. For example, JS might raise event 2 before event 1 finished processing, and by the time event 1 is done, there might not even be an event 2 handler any more and then you have an error.\r\n\r\n### Why we're only just encountering this now\r\n\r\n1. We didn't have multithreading before\r\n2. Even to the extent that we did have an early preview of multithreading, it worked by running .NET on the browser UI thread, so we could define that as the sync context and then all the same assumptions would remain valid within that sync context. But now .NET WebAssembly has just moved to the new \"deputy thread\" multithreading model (i.e., all .NET code is on a background worker), these assumptions are no longer valid (e.g., because the UI thread's JS can no longer communicate with .NET in a synchronous, blocking manner).\r\n\r\n### Ensuring correctness\r\n\r\nWe've already solved all these problems in our other hosting environments, Server and WebView, because they've always been innately asynchronous from the beginning. We would need to generalize/port all these mechanisms so they are shared with or copied by the WebAssembly renderer, JS interop, eventing system, etc.:\r\n\r\n- [ ] Change rendering to serialize renderbatches to JS instead of doing shared-memory reads\r\n- [ ] Change the rendering flow so that the renderer's `UpdateDisplayAsync` returns a `Task` that doesn't complete until the JS side sends back an explicit acknowledgement of that renderbatch\r\n- [ ] Review JS interop to make sure any low-level assumptions we've made about synchrony during the internals of message passing are replaced by async assumptions\r\n- [ ] Do the above without changing things for the **single-threaded** WebAssembly flavour, since (1) it would be breaking if for example synchronous UI updates became async, and (2) those perf optimizations are there for a reason, and we don't want to make rendering many times more expensive in cases where you'd be serializing huge strings, for example. It's OK to have significant behavioral and performance changes when people opt into multithreading, but not when they don't.\r\n\r\n### Approach\r\n\r\nAs a broad strategy, I think we can:\r\n\r\n * Factor out some new `WebRenderer` subclass called something like `AsyncWebRenderer` that holds the common logic around serializing renderbatches and accepting the async renderbatch acknowledgements from JS. This can then be used by all of Server, WebView, and multithreaded-WebAssembly.\r\n * Use our WebView implementation as the reference for how a complete, async-safe rendering and eventing model should work, because this was more recently implemented than Server and is generally simpler and cleaner. There's not a huge amount of code in it, really. If some extra work is needed to queue event notifications, for example, we should see that clearly from the WebView code.\r\n\r\nI suspect it's not necessary to have two different builds of `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly`. The total amount of code that should differ between the threaded and not-threaded won't be very much. I expect we can just have two different `Renderer` subclasses and some if/else branches in the JS Background and Motivation\n\nWe want to support ahead-of-time compilation for the **Aspire Dashboard**, and the framework support that requires from Blazor does not exist yet. This proposal is that support.\n\nBlazor discovers a great deal about an application at runtime. Which components exist and how to construct them; which of their members are parameters, and how to read and write each one; which members carry `[Inject]` and what service each wants; which members of a model are reachable through `@bind`; which methods are `[JSInvokable]` and how to dispatch to them; and how to serialize the values flowing through all of the above. Today every one of those questions is answered by walking `MemberInfo` and invoking reflectively, and the JSON carrying the values is serialized through the reflection-based contract resolver.\n\nAll of that information is knowable at compile time. The Razor compiler already sees the component graph; the attributes are already there in source. What is missing is a way for a source generator to write that knowledge down, and a way for the framework to use it when it is available.\n\nThat is what this API is: **a contract between generated code and the framework, describing what the framework currently discovers by reflection.** When an application supplies it, Blazor reads parameters, resolves injectables, walks bind models, dispatches JS interop and serializes state through ordinary generated code. When it is absent, nothing changes and the existing reflection paths run exactly as before.\n\nThe Dashboard is what has driven the shape here — it is a real application that exercises all of these paths at once, which is why we used it to validate the design rather than a synthetic sample. But nothing in this API is specific to it: any Blazor Server application can supply the same metadata, and applications that stay JIT-compiled benefit too, through less runtime discovery, less metadata kept alive for trimming, and serialization that no longer depends on reflection being enabled.\n\nBecause generated code lives in the **application's own assembly**, every type and member it touches has to be public. That is why this proposal is as large as it is. Nothing here is meant to be written by hand: an application author adds a single call, `AddComponentMetadata\u003cTContext\u003e()`, and the generator produces the rest. The types sit in `*.Infrastructure` namespaces, and everything proposed here carries `[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\")]` so the shape can still move while we take more applications through it.\n\n## Proposed API\n\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components` — what the generator writes down\n\n```diff\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Infrastructure;\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class ComponentDescriptor\n+{\n+    public Type Type { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cIServiceProvider, IComponent\u003e? CreateInstance { get; init; }\n+    public IReadOnlyList\u003cComponentParameterDescriptor\u003e Parameters { get; init; }\n+    public IReadOnlyList\u003cComponentInjectableDescriptor\u003e Injectables { get; init; }\n+    public IReadOnlyList\u003cobject\u003e Metadata { get; init; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class ComponentParameterDescriptor\n+{\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\n+    public Type ParameterType { get; init; }\n+    public Attribute Attribute { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cobject, object?\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\n+    public Action\u003cobject, object?\u003e SetValue { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cIServiceProvider, object?\u003e? GetStateSerializer { get; init; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class ComponentInjectableDescriptor\n+{\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\n+    public Type ServiceType { get; init; }\n+    public InjectAttribute Attribute { get; init; }\n+    public Action\u003cobject, object?\u003e SetValue { get; init; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class BindableTypeDescriptor\n+{\n+    public Type Type { get; init; }\n+    public IReadOnlyList\u003cBindableMemberDescriptor\u003e Members { get; init; }\n+    public IReadOnlyList\u003cBindableIndexerDescriptor\u003e Indexers { get; init; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class BindableMemberDescriptor\n+{\n+    public string Name { get; init; }\n+    public Type MemberType { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cobject, object?\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class BindableIndexerDescriptor\n+{\n+    public Type IndexType { get; init; }\n+    public Type ValueType { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cobject, object?, object?\u003e GetValue { get; init; }\n+}\n```\n\n### `Microsoft.JSInterop` — described `[JSInvokable]` dispatch\n\n```diff\nnamespace Microsoft.JSInterop.Infrastructure;\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public sealed class JSInvokableMethodDescriptor\n+{\n+    public string Identifier { get; init; }\n+    public string AssemblyName { get; init; }\n+    public Type TargetType { get; init; }\n+    public Func\u003cobject?, string, JsonSerializerOptions, ValueTask\u003cstring?\u003e\u003e Invoke { get; init; }\n+}\n\nnamespace Microsoft.JSInterop;\n\npublic abstract class JSRuntime\n{\n+    [Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+    protected virtual IReadOnlyList\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\u003e? InvokableMethods { get; }\n}\n```\n\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web` — the aggregate and its registration\n\n```diff\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web;\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public abstract class RazorComponentsMetadataContext\n+{\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\u003cComponentDescriptor\u003e Components { get; }\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\u003cBindableTypeDescriptor\u003e BindableTypes { get; }\n+    public abstract IReadOnlyList\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\u003e JSInvokableMethods { get; }\n+    public abstract IJsonTypeInfoResolver? JsonTypeInfoResolver { get; }\n+}\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Assembly, AllowMultiple = true)]\n+public sealed class BindableModelAttribute : Attribute\n+{\n+    public Type ModelType { get; init; }\n+}\n\nnamespace Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public static class ComponentMetadataServiceCollectionExtensions\n+{\n+    public static IServiceCollection AddComponentMetadata\u003cTContext\u003e(this IServiceCollection services)\n+        where TContext : RazorComponentsMetadataContext, new();\n+}\n```\n\n### `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server` — describing how a type is stored\n\nThe one piece here that is written by hand rather than generated.\n\n```diff\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.ProtectedBrowserStorage;\n\n+[Experimental(\"ASPNETCORE9004\", UrlFormat = \"https://aka.ms/aspnet/analyzer/{0}\")]\n+public abstract class ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\u003cT\u003e\n+{\n+    protected ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer();\n+    public abstract string Serialize(T value);\n+    public abstract T Deserialize(string data);\n+}\n\npublic abstract class ProtectedBrowserStorage\n{\n+    public ValueTask SetAsync\u003cTValue\u003e(string key, TValue value);\n+    public ValueTask SetAsync\u003cTValue\u003e(string purpose, string key, TValue value);\n}\n```\n\nThe `SetAsync\u003cTValue\u003e` overloads are deliberately **not** experimental. Overload resolution prefers them over the existing `SetAsync(string, object)` whenever the argument's static type is more specific than `object`, so marking them would raise a diagnostic on existing, unmodified call sites that never opt into a serializer. With no serializer registered they behave exactly as the object-typed overloads do; opting in requires touching `ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\u003cT\u003e`, which is where the diagnostic belongs.\n\n## Usage Examples\n\n**What an application author writes.** One line, plus a `[BindableModel]` assembly attribute for any model reached through `@bind` that the generator cannot infer from the component graph alone:\n\n```csharp\nvar builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);\n\nbuilder.Services.AddRazorComponents().AddInteractiveServerComponents();\nbuilder.Services.AddComponentMetadata\u003cAppMetadata\u003e();   // AppMetadata is generated\n```\n\n**What the generator emits** (abbreviated — this is the shape the contract has to support):\n\n```csharp\ninternal sealed partial class AppMetadata : RazorComponentsMetadataContext\n{\n    public override IReadOnlyList\u003cComponentDescriptor\u003e Components { get; } =\n    [\n        new ComponentDescriptor\n        {\n            Type = typeof(Counter),\n            CreateInstance = static _ =\u003e new Counter(),\n            Parameters =\n            [\n                new ComponentParameterDescriptor\n                {\n                    Name = \"IncrementAmount\",\n                    ParameterType = typeof(int),\n                    Attribute = new ParameterAttribute(),\n                    GetValue = static c =\u003e ((Counter)c).IncrementAmount,\n                    SetValue = static (c, v) =\u003e ((Counter)c).IncrementAmount = (int)v!,\n                },\n            ],\n            Injectables = [ /* ... */ ],\n            Metadata = [ /* ... */ ],\n        },\n    ];\n\n    public override IReadOnlyList\u003cJSInvokableMethodDescriptor\u003e JSInvokableMethods { get; } =\n    [\n        new JSInvokableMethodDescriptor\n        {\n            Identifier = \"NotifyResize\",\n            AssemblyName = \"Dashboard\",\n            TargetType = typeof(ResizeListener),\n            Invoke = static (target, json, options) =\u003e /* generated deserialize + call */,\n        },\n    ];\n\n    public override IJsonTypeInfoResolver? JsonTypeInfoResolver =\u003e AppJsonContext.Default;\n}\n```\n\n**The hand-written piece.** A type stored in protected local storage that has no JSON contract:\n\n```csharp\npublic sealed class ThemeSerializer : ProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\u003cTheme\u003e\n{\n    public override string Serialize(Theme value) =\u003e value.Name;\n\n    public override Theme Deserialize(string data) =\u003e new(data);\n}\n```\n\n```csharp\nbuilder.Services.AddSingleton\u003cProtectedBrowserStorageSerializer\u003cTheme\u003e, ThemeSerializer\u003e();\n```\n\n```csharp\n@inject ProtectedLocalStorage Storage\n\nawait Storage.SetAsync(\"theme\", new Theme(\"solarized\"));\n\nvar result = await Storage.GetAsync\u003cTheme\u003e(\"theme\");\n```\n\n## Alternative .NET trimmer statically analyzes your project and removes any unused code. In Blazor we use the .NET trimmer to significantly reduce the publish size of Blazor WebAssembly apps. However, we don't currently use the .NET trimmer to its fullest potential. We currently configure the trimmer in a partial mode, which only trims assemblies that are explicitly marked as trimmable. This typically means that the app assembly itself and many dependencies are not trimmed. This is a conservative setting that optimizes for maintaining functionality over reducing app size. \r\n\r\nThe default trim mode for the .NET trimmer is to trim everything. This is the mode used by the .NET Native AOT workloads.Analyzers provide warnings if there are code paths in the app that are not safe to trim. Given how sensitive web apps are to download size and load time, it seems like doing full trimming should be the goal for Blazor.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full trimming also is a potential solution to enabling a [single project model for Blazor Web Apps](#49079) that target both server and browser. When you multitarget a project, everything in the project is built for both targets unless you indicated otherwise. This is problematic for browser scenarios because you may potentially bring in dependencies, components, and code into the browser targeted build that are only needed on the server. However, if we could enable full trimming *and* indicate to the trimmer which components are setup to render on WebAssembly, then the browser build could be aggressively trimmed to remove any unwanted code and dependencies.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full .NET trimming typically means removing any dynamic code path that are based on reflection. We would need to make Blazor apps trimmer friendly by removing this code using techniques like source generators. For example, in Blazor we use reflection as part of the component discovery process and in the render tree builder code generated by the Razor compiler. We're already working on enabling [component discovery through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/48767). We also have on our backlog to [handle component parameters through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/29550). There may be other related work items as well.\r\n\r\nThere is also ecosystem impact of enabling full trimming by default. Many .NET libraries are not setup for trimming and would potentially need to be updated. It will take some time to work through these issues with the Blazor community. Certain features also simply wouldn't work with full trimming. For example, dynamically loading dependencies at runtime that are not known statically. For backwards compatibility, app developers can configure the trimmer to not trim assemblies that are not yet trimmer friendly. We'd need to understand better all the cases that get impacted by full trimming and ensure we provide a reasonable user experience for addressing The \"weather forecast\" page simply generates data on the client and thus only demonstrates how to render a table, not how to fetch data.\r\n\r\nActually calling a server API in all generality, accounting for all the main ways of setting up a site, is complicated by several factors, as pointed out by @mrpmorris:\r\n\r\n * Deal with prerendering or auto mode. In these cases, you have to be able to load the data when running on WebAssembly *and* when running on the server. So you must either:\r\n   * Register `HttpClient` in DI with a base address on both server and client, and have the server call itself via HTTP\r\n   * Or, have some interface representing the datastore, and set up both server and client implementations\r\n * Avoid the double-render problem whereby the data is loaded twice (once for prerendering, once for interactivity)\r\n   * This is more complicated with per-page interactivity, since enanced nav doesn't currently work with persistent state\r\n * Make this work sensibly with auth, including for both client and server data access\r\n\r\nWhile typical apps don't usually have to solve all these problems simultaneously, we need to be able to demonstrate convenient, flexible patterns that do compose well with all the features and are clean enough to put them in the project template.\r\n\r\nSolving this nicely likely depends on implementing some other features like https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/51584\r\n\r\n# Note for community: Recommendation for .NET 8 developers\r\n\r\nAs mentioned above, typical apps don't normally have to solve all these problems. It's always been simple to load data from the server with Blazor WebAssembly and that is still the case in .NET 8.\r\n\r\nThe easiest path is simply to disable WebAssembly prerendering, because then just about all the complexity vanishes. Whenever you used rendermode `WebAssembly` (e.g., in `App.razor`), replace it with `new WebAssemblyRenderMode(prerender: false)`.\r\n\r\nAt that point your UI is just running in the browser and you can make `HttpClient` calls to the server as
